title: The Caro-Kann Advance
standfirst: The Caro-Kann is the French with the bad bishop problem solved. Same plans for White, one important difference — and the difference is the whole reason people play it.

steps.title: The French, fixed
body: In the French, Black plays 1…e6 to support …d5 and buries the c8 bishop behind it. The Caro-Kann supports …d5 with the c-pawn instead, leaving the bishop's diagonal open.
One pawn on a different square. Everything else about the structure is the same.

steps.title: Support d5 without blocking anything
body: The move that defines the opening. It prepares …d5 exactly as …e6 does in the French — but the c8 bishop still has somewhere to go.

steps.title: The confrontation
body: And as in the French, White must now decide.

steps.title: Advance — same plan as against the French
body: Space, locked centre, play on the wings. If you already know the French Advance you know White's plan here: hold d4, gain kingside space, attack.

steps.title: Out first — this is the entire point
body: Here it is. In the French, this bishop spends the game staring at its own pawn. In the Caro-Kann it steps outside before the e-pawn boxes it in.
This is why some players prefer the Caro-Kann to the French despite the extra tempo it costs. One good bishop is worth a move.

steps.title: Develop and prepare
body: White gets on with it, heading for a kingside build-up.

steps.title: Now the pawn can go there safely
body: Only after the bishop is out. Same pawn, same square, completely different position — the order is the whole idea.

steps.title: Quiet and flexible
body: White develops modestly, keeping options open.

steps.title: The familiar lever
body: The same plan as the French: attack the base of the d4–e5 chain. Black's counterplay is identical here — it's only his pieces that are better placed.

steps.title: Hold the base with a piece
body: Another way to defend d4, developing at the same time.

steps.title: Same battle, better bishop
body: The structures are the same as the French Advance; put the two final positions side by side and the only real difference is where Black's light-squared bishop lives.
That difference decides the game. Learn structures, not move orders — you now understand two openings for the price of one.
